Changing status to a more accurate state.

In the disappeared virtual world of Twinity, places could be rated from 1 to 5 stars and a note of the visit could be left, usually with compliments about the place. These notes could be a great idea, since they encouraged creativity.

Analytics are important and need more data:

We need to know:

- Durations: How long are people staying? are they joining and leaving?

- Heatmaps: Where are they hanging out? Are they standing at spawn or can they find the social areas, which social areas are underperforming?

- Player counts: Is the world at capacity most of the time, should I add or less player slots for best fit

- Performance and Hardware: Are quest players getting lower frames, do they need more tuning, are certain brands of GPUs having issues, is desktop performance worse than VR?

- - Do android users have more RAM than I thought, do they need a battery saving setting for the world?

- - Is my world the issue or avatars the performance bottleneck?

- World Visiters: Is a majority of my playtime repeat guests or 1 time visitors

- - Is it easy for visitors to stay longer, is there player retention issues by player experience or rank

- Location: Is a majority of my visitors from Japan or Mexico? 

- - Should I spend time to add multilingual options?

- Time Zones: are players visiting my maps during the weekdays or do they only get on for "drinking" nights on weekends? What are the peak times to do a multi-instance event?

- Player Feedback: Did the players like or dislike, what was their total time at review

I'd like more accurate demographic info:

- Age

- Nationality

- Rank (are more new players joining, or more trusted users?)

If I find something surprising, like an uptick in users from Canada and France, that may promote the need for a French translation that I can't currently see right now. When I ask about ages on group tours, they tend to be much older (30+). It'd be good to have that broken down in a line graph somehow, to see where they rise, where they peak, where they fall off.

title: Disapointed
details:
I got into VRC about last Christmas. I wanted to make avatars, and that needed unity. I had never really done anything with coding or modeling. So I setout to learn unity by the tutorials, and a month later I had a basic 3d pacman game, which I wanted to make a world even though I knew at the time C# was blacklisted. Then I heard about playmaker excitedly bought that. Its a total pain in the ass... But I converted all my C# and more to playmaker eventually. There are not really specific details as to why they didn't go with playmaker. Its crappy but it does work. The thing is though, VRC script is terrible. I would rather drive a nail through my own foreskin. Because at least C# and playmaker have documentation and a community already. VRC script is just hoping you glean tidbits from people you run into with very slim documentation or examples. Or if they are out there, are not centrally linked. 


I have put a lot of time into my pacman world and I am hopeful these VRC graphs will have the tools to do what I need. But the biggest problem I foresee is that there are complex tools unity has published on GitHub that might not be possible. My world depends on 2 of them.


So if you guys seriously plan on doing this I want to see docs, with examples.

Edit: and for the argument of playmaker being the lynch pin holding things together because its 1 guy... We are still on unity 5.6.3p, which unity stopped developing.

title: Community plugins (Custom Udon Graph nodes)
details:
This community is very creative and no matter how many resources you put towards building cool tools, you will always lag behind the community's ideas.

As such I think having some type of experimental area where world builders can extend the Node Graph without being blacklisted during upload seems like a great way to me to propose new features.

Simple text and screenshots in the canny don't seem adequate for me here because you can't test your code, nor can you really illustrate properly what the benefits are.

For example, what if you wish to build a PA / microphone system leveraging runtime modifications of the spatial audio parameters?

This requires that you test with other players to get it right. And the best way to present the results would be through a demo.

Now imagine someone could build a custom node for the Node Graph along the lines of:

Set Audio Parameters

- Audio source

- Min range

- Max range

...

And you're able to reference player voices as the audio source here, perhaps through a trigger of sorts.

comments.body: This would be nice as sort of a choice thing, i myself cant get much out of the shortened term. But i do understand what the individual steps do

I think the bottom line of any thing other than Pure C# is that it wont be as efficient or smooth as using C#. It was the same way in playmaker. I converted a script with 1 real line of code into 4 actions and like 3 variables.

Still I share your frustration that other solutions have already worked a lot of bugs out. Where with something brand new, There will probably be 3 patches in the first month. And it will take a year to probably even get it in the first place.

Custom nodes of our own C# needs to be a thing or this is not a serious scripting solution. I use Blueprints extensively in Unreal engine, and the ability to write your own nodes is paramount to the usability of that system.  At the very least we need to be able to take chunks of code and "Group" them into functions with input and output chains.

I don't think this will (or should) ever happen. I want scriptign as much as anyone, but there are just too many security and exploitation concerns. Node based programming is less efficient and more constrained, but good enough for VRChat.
We will have an official route to make nodes from custom compilers like Udon#
After Udon 2 has been launched publicly, we'd planning to work on a feature to allow the creation of custom Graph nodes!

title: String manipulations
details:
I'm trying to extend the keyboard from "Tell Your Word" by Kanata and found there's no sensible way to manipulate strings within the SDK, so keystrokes are sent to the webpanel instead.

Please be sure Node Graph includes at least a couple of these:

Concatenation
Joining (i.e. take an array of strings and put them together with a separator)
Slicing (aka substrings)
Upper / lower case

Templating (i.e. "foo {input} baz", with input bar gives "foo bar baz")

Regex replacements (for example escaping special characters)

Regex pattern and group matching (for example to grab a youtube video ID out of a link, but only if it's a youtube link)

Decoding and Encoding some important formats. Like HTML entities (UI text could use this for example) and URL parameters (for web panels).

Some predefined character sets to validate against:
Alphanumerical, ASCII, etc.

I'm sure I'm still forgetting a few.

comments.body: This should all be possible with Udon now!

title: Fine grained Data Syncing
details:
Currently buffered triggers and object sync are the only primitives we have for tackling syncing issues ourselves.

This results in unholy amounts of boilerplate involving animations, controllers and blank objects filled with triggers (typically onEnable) to track simple values like an integer reliably and efficiently. You can forget about strings.

The data that flows through these graphs need syncing options, as well as a simple and deterministic thread safety model once you're able to receive values from the network. Such as an event loop.

title: Allow world creators to change Physics bounce threshold
details:
Physics simulations in VRChat are limited in realism because creators can't modify most of the variables in physics settings.

For example, I'm working on a mini golf map and my golf balls stick to walls at low speeds rather than bouncing off realistically. I've gotten the editor's simulation to look nearly 1:1 with real golf balls by changing the "Bounce Threshold" in the PhysicsManager to 0. However, these changes do not carry over when I'm testing the map in VRChat.

I can maybe understand restricting the solver iterations to prevent lag, but even then it should be up to creators to optimize their worlds. If the physics settings can be made changeable it would be very appreciated!

 https://feedback.vrchat.com/feature-requests/p/sdk-feature-add-support-for-setting-bounce-threshold

(also had people start vrchat at 5hz to drive through walls, or 1000hz to win a speed challenge)

title: Moderation Tools for World Creators
details:
Allow world creators the ability to moderate their OWN worlds and issue their OWN bans. I'm tired of seeing crashers and exploiters in my worlds and kicking them is nothing. I want the ability to ban certain individuals from my worlds. 

There is absolutely no harm in doing this. Who is it going to hurt? The exploiters and cheaters.

What if world creators abuse it and ban people from THEIR OWN worlds? Well it's their fault their world fails to gather a population.

What else will this do? Allow world creators to suit the needs of their wanted audience. 

it will also help take the stress off of the actually game moderators. 

Thank you,
Lucifer MStar - Creator of 30+ worlds including church of marriages. 

P.S. Communicate more with your community on what you are doing about these crashers and exploiters and maybe the heat and stress will die down. Honestly this is the most annoying thing communication.

comments.body: If the suggested feature is implemented, world creators will be held responsible for moderating witch hunts that are unrelated to their world's activity, even though they may lack the qualifications, experience, or skills to do so. This combined with Sasha Mason's concerns about sharing bans, which have already shown mixed results on a small scale, makes it evident that the difficulties of implementing this feature far outweigh any potential benefits.

The Museum's biggest rule, please respect the artists and their time, is meant to ensure the personal safety of all contributors. Artists and contributors shouldn't get flooded with hate, harassment, threats, or excessive popularity. In return, they're willing to contribute and have their art and history displayed for free, and the project can operate. I tell people of my mod powers, and they feel more secure having their names and history displayed. When trolls first found my world and realized I had the power to kick anyone in any public instance, they asked me to stop joining public lobbies. When they realized these powers are built into VRC, they stopped.

I join instances opened by others. TheDoctor26 (creator of Furhub and Furhub Karaoke) opened the instance where I held Sylys' memorial on the day of his passing. While relaying his life's history, I knew not everyone would approve. But because I had mod powers, I felt more at-ease not having to take 80 people to a new instance just to ensure history could be told accurately. And I did remove someone that night who harassed me in that instance.

World creators who abuse their powers aren't benefiting their world. But because full details of mod actions aren't publicly shared, mods already have to put up with harassment from people who know less about the reasoning behind such actions, and any Canny request to eliminate mod powers undercuts moderation even further. Mods need more help to ensure peace, not less.

I can say any decision to remove mod tools from world creators will absolutely hurt the museum. And since world creators have a vested interest in the worlds they create, their powers are less likely to be used for petty reasons and more likely to be used to curtail trolling, hatemongering, and bad actors of all sorts.

@{62e1e57a8ec14e44acda4664|full_name}: So, aside from the difficulty of moving 80 players from a normal public instance to a group public instance, there is no reason for you to have these world author moderation powers? I don't know your world or your exact use-cares, but we can find better ways to solve these issues.

Sounds like we just need ways to change the ownership of an existing instance. So you can convert a normal public instance into a group public instance.

Or maybe a more reliable way to move a massive number of people between instances. For example a way to automatically invite everyone in an instance to a new instance or something. Probably something like a "party system" would be best here, so you can join a party and have an easier time following them between instances.

The last and arguable most effective options are already built-in to VRChat. Everyone has the ability to mute or block people that are being a nuisance. And if that isn't enough, a vote-to-kick can be called on the troublemaker.

Either way, these are just random first ideas that could potentially solve the issues you are describing, which would allow the new groups features to take over where the old "world author moderation powers" have clearly failed.

Some of the worst world authors seem to be so entitled that they think they should be able to enter any private instances of their world, or that they should be immune to group moderation actions while in group public instances of their world. And this is all just so they can prevent a few people they have labeled as "bad" from using their published world.

@{610d538d5303a82960a415b4|full_name} NO. If world creators can't moderate public instances, it will just lead to creators never wanting to use Public instances ever again. There is a deep, longstanding record of very lousy trolls doxxing, harassing, and spreading false rumors targetting Furries. Any attempt to limit world creators' abilities will give those trolls more power. Some people use information in the worlds to benefit their own hatemongering schemes and have broken trust completely. This is not 1 in 10 people, or even 1 in 100, this is 1 in 10,000. Those people pose an immediate danger and threat to the safety of users and break trust with the platform. We can give information to VRChat's Trust and Safety team, but without any ability to moderate public instances, World Creators would become powerless to help people immediately when known abusers are permitted free reign. The good far outweighs the bad on this decision. World creators who abuse their powers can and should be reported, and after investigations it would make sense to remove them. But known harassers and abusers can't wait for a decision from the TOS team to stop harassing people in an instance. One of my friends recorded such an interaction and submitted it to VRChat.

People salty about world creator's moderation are just salty about moderation in general.  Until VRChat finds some magic way to eliminate trolls, my vote will always be for better moderation. And nothing anyone says will justify a world creator's inability to remove known dangerous and psychotic individuals from spreading rumors, ripping avatars, crashing lobbies, etc. in a public instance of their own world.

@{62e1e57a8ec14e44acda4664|full_name}:

> "NO. If world creators can't moderate public instances, it will just lead to creators never wanting to use Public instances ever again."

Plenty of people don't like normal public instances for any number of reasons. I don't see why the world author/creator should be treated any differently.

But I will agree that normal public instances would be without any moderation at all. I just don't see that as a bad thing currently. Maybe because I haven't seen all the same things you have. I didn't mean to be insensitive or anything.

> "Those people pose an immediate danger and threat to the safety of users and break trust with the platform."

Then you, as the world author, kicking them from a single public instance doesn't make a difference. You should make a detailed report to VRChat's Trust and Safety, so they can be dealt with correctly and potentially permanently.

> "World creators who abuse their powers can and should be reported, and after investigations it would make sense to remove them."

I agree, but we are still waiting to see these reports actually leading to any sort of action.

> "People salty about world creator's moderation are just salty about moderation in general."

I think you are missing the scope of current world author moderation powers. The world creator has moderation powers in ALL instances of their world. If a vindictive world creator wanted to, they could assert their will unto any instance they manage to enter. For example, if a world creator could enter a friends+ instance owned by someone they dislike, they could join and literally kick the instance owner out instantly. The same is true for group public instances, the world creator also has moderation powers there, which has caused moderation wars where the groups are forced to ban the world creator from their group just to prevent them from joining.

I would be happy enough if the world creator moderation powers were just limited to only be in normal public instances. That way everything will seem consistent with the rest of VRChat, and we won't have to worry about moderation wars. VRChat can then take their time to decide what they want to do with moderation of normal public instances in due time. Simply just prevent world creators from asserting their moderation on instances they don't own.

@{610d538d5303a82960a415b4|full_name} You may not have had experience with this, but many have. Some world creators and moderators experienced attacks, harassment, defamation, and doxxing by trolls in their world. Trolls who use alt accounts to bypass bans regularly. Restraining abilities to moderate public instances makes VRChat's public instances that much more unsafe for people.

Blocking people does not stop them from sending defamation, death threats, and swat threats. Ensuring they are at least unallowed in the worlds of the creators they hurt is the first step in making sure that behavior gets controlled.

If a world creator cannot guarantee safety in their own world, then what will supplement this lack of safety?

@{62e1e57a8ec14e44acda4664|full_name}:

> "If a world creator cannot guarantee safety in their own world, then what will supplement this lack of safety?"

The players (or world creators themselves) can make a new instance, preferably a group public instance so they can moderate it themselves and feel safe. Or they can go to a private instance if they want to be even safer.

If you want to encourage people that visit your world to use group public instances of your official group, so you can moderate it better, then look at how the Trans Academy does it. If you enter a normal public instance of their world, it has a message explaining that it is unmoderated and suggest that people move to an instance hosted by the official group.
here to say I was the 1000th vote I did my part.

I 100% support this idea, I have seen people in this game breaking TOS in public worlds, including cases of pedophilia and I know for a fact they also use my worlds for roleplay purposes. I do not want to incentivise these people to be in VRChat, I would like to ban  them permanently from using any of my worlds.

The VRChat RP community (especially the Genshin Impact one) is full of pedophiles looking to prey on minors and as a world creator I want to ban users I know are involved into this type of ilegal acts, I got a long list of users I wish to  permanently ban from my worlds because they have openly broken VRChat TOS and commited US federal crimes in front of me.

Honestly its insane we still don't have a proper system for this and they straight up have a rule against preemptively moderating people. Like what if world creators just don't want certain people and groups in their world because they're being a nuisance to everyone. It'd make the game much better for everyone if world creators could actually self moderate their own worlds.

@{621afb77c20d153ae60791a9|full_name} I believe at some point I've suggested giving world creators an ability to, at least, ban groups. It would give the "Block the Group" button more purpose than just blocking incoming invites. Which would be fair, considering that a ton of groups powertrip, but it only got one comment saying "No, this is dumb, world creators already have too much power", but I digress. 

Along with being able to check for age verification through Udon, it'd make moderation by world creators extremely effective. And as MStar pointed out, if a world creator bans people left and right as well - it's on them that their world flops.

@{5e607dc532f5e02bee5f7f2f|full_name} I don't think straight up NSFW content should be allowed on a 13+ platform period. Will that happen? Probably not with the current leadership.

I like your idea of being able to ban certain groups. I'd personally make a whole list of nsfw/gooner groups that VRChat isn't dealing with and completely ban them from my world.

Use Predictive Analysis:

- Known Crasher AV

- AV Statistics that are outside norms.

- Known Crasher Group or Groups that do not align

- Suspect Account

- VR Chat Management that actually cares about the community and proactively looks at System Metrics to trap and remove disruptive users.

Oh, or just use toolsets like VRCx or TailGrab to help you do what VR Chat will not..

Linking to this other feedback request which expresses a similar sentiment.

It's definitely important, especially now with World Persistence, that world creators should be able to protect their own worlds from bad actors.

https://feedback.vrchat.com/feature-requests/p/world-persistence-and-game-integrity

My thinking is that the ToS for Udon-powered world moderation as currently written was well-suited before worlds could have persistence, but now that worlds can be powered by persistence, it is time to re-evaluate the ToS and create rules that account for cheaters able to misbehave in one instance and carry that result with them into new instances where the ToS does not currently allow creators to do anything about it.

As a world creator for 4 years, I totally agree. Especially with the persistence-data update, relying on assigned moderators to regulate players is nearly impossible to protect the economy of the game worlds with any kind of trade system. 

I understand many would worry about the "can't play with friends " issue. But having a tool that allows world creators to restrict certain players from entering public instances of their worlds can still be a huge help. Banned players can still join their friends+ instances or other private instances. With this system, we can minimize the damage that can be caused by every mod client abuser and exploiter. 

I genuinely believe this system could greatly improve the atmosphere of game worlds, while it doesn't harm any player's needs. For streamers who want to host events, they can host with group instance or friends+, there's no restriction for anyone to enjoy the world, but also giving a chance for the world creator to moderate and make their world a better place.

In the ideal world, world authors are just designers, and VRChat Inc. ban all cheaters with cheat detection.

But evidently, VRChat Inc. is not effective nor efficient at policing cheaters. Perhaps because VRChat itself takes a fairly lenient approach to cheat detection (e.g. multiboxing is allowed lol) due to it being fundamentally a chat room with a fancy 3D interface rather than a serious game engine.

Imo it should be entirely VRChat's responsibility to up their cheat detection standard and treat their game more like a game.

User level moderation should be moderating user level problems, like someone pisses someone off, or breaking some social rules in the lobby.

User level moderation (or Udon moderation tools) should never have to tackle program level or hacking related problems, because that is a program level violation that is VRChat Inc.'s domain.

Therefore, giving world authors more "anti-hack" is a mere patchwork that does not resolve the underlying causes of the problem.

The more fundamental solution would be VRChat Inc. completely pivoting to a zero tolerance approach to anti-cheat, with better cheat detection and automatic logging/reporting and banning, better reporting or voting functions, disallow multiboxing etc. (just like any other serious multiplayer games).

There is a fundamental philosophical disagreement here, between a chat room program (easy) and a game engine/platform (hard). VRChat Inc. needs to make up their mind, and up their game.

@{67a0ed8d6e7354cc8f8c7acd|full_name} Just like how VRChat allows group instance owners and moderators ban people that they never want to see in their instances. We can't ask VRChat to actively monitor every published world 24/7. There are so many of them. And every game world has different conditions to consider.

For example, attached is a shop of a guy selling exploited in-game currency in my poker world. I know exactly who he is, and I really want to stop him from doing that. But reporting him to the VRChat Safety team probably won't help that much because this isn't typically a violation of the VRChat ToS. The best thing in this case I can do is just ignore and let them grow. It's really upsetting for me as a world creator to watch it burn.

Having a persistent system really made moderating game worlds a different story. Especially for the games that involve PVP or an in-game resource transfer system.

@{66035290730e0be239bc91c3|full_name}, in my case it started with just one bad apple. One world creator trying to do everything in their power to prevent some players from even being in their world, for silly drama reasons.

This is just not how VRChat is supposed to be currently. Worlds are supposed to be available for everyone, and groups are supposed to be the layer on top that moderates the instances with Group Public and Group+ instances.

So I will voice my opinion in that direction, untill VRChat decides to change their whole philosophy on instance/world moderation. VRChat however has seemed reluctant to make changes here so far.

comments.body:
I found implementations that provide networking events with optional parameters, but I did not check yet if it works:

https://github.com/tutinoco/SimpleNetworkUdonBehaviour

https://github.com/Miner28/NetworkedEventCaller

One of the uses of SendCustomNetworkEvent is to change the variables of the other person's object. SendCustomNetworkEvent with optional parameters can simplify your code in the uses.

When you need to change a variable of an object which you do not own, you cannot simply change the variable, like "x=1;".

You can use "SendCustomNetworkEvent" but it does not support parameters. If you knew the variable x takes few possibility (like x is only 0, 1, 2, ..., 32), you can imprement functions named "SetXto0", "SetXto1", "SetXto2", ..., "SetXto32" and make the owner change the variable through "SendCustomNetworkEvent(VRC.Udon.Common.Interfaces.NetworkEventTarget.Owner, 'SetXto0')". This system works but loses readability.

I found several posts on twitter using SendCustomNetworkEvent in a mentioned way:

https://twitter.com/kohack_v/status/1545084516339175425

https://twitter.com/LefTonbo/status/1308000053001240576

https://twitter.com/bironist/status/1278194376930234369

If you can fire SendCustomNetworkEvent with optional parameters, you need to implement just one function like "SetX(int x)". This method is also compatible with other values than 0~32.
It honestly blows my mind that Udon basically has functions but doesn't allow for arguments. How is that not one of the most basic features there on day 1?
Stupidly this is proven to be entirely possible since U# can do this perfectly fine

Will note that you can kinda do this by extending OnDeserialization() where when you sync a variable you can then call a function and pass it that new synced variable. That said this only works with variables you can sync with udon and would be much cleaner if we could just pass a variable with a custom event.
Had always been eager to see this feature. Currently even the simplest integer arg, i have to work around by adding them to name of the event listener function.
It's absolutely insane that I can't just put variables into functions...

If you're only looking for argument support on SendCustomEvent in U#, I made a package to add support for that:

https://github.com/NGenesis/UdonCustomEventArgs
Finally, we will have it! https://ask.vrchat.com/t/developer-update-april-24-2025/43071#p-78906-upcoming-udon-network-events-with-parameters-9

Is it possible to add SendCustomEvent and SendCustomEventDelayed with parameters to the official SDK? I am very grateful that Genesis implemented one, but I also hope the development team could consider including those functions in official SDK for better compatibility with future SDK releases.

The reason I want these functions is that although the newly released networked version covers many use cases, it does not allow non-syncable arguments, like object references. I am trying to make an event system where event calls are broadcasted to multiple receivers that come in different classes, and I want to pass object references to them as event context.

details:
Think of it as a way of commenting out a node while leaving it in your code structure.

Useful for debugging. Like in the case where you don't want to reconnect a bunch of noodles to check if taking the node out fixes your bug.

Or if you are one to horde commented out code you will appreciate it too.

A more complicated version of the feature would _optionally_ allow commenting out the node, but allowing flow to continue. But, I dunno if that is just crazy.
title: [Request] A way to "Disable" a node while keeping it all noodled up with other active nodes

comments.body: If you disable the node, what happens to the node after it? Like if you have 3 nodes, with a noodle flowing through them... and you disable the middle node.. does the 3rd node still get executed? Or do you want a chain reaction, where disabling a node, stops all further execution in the noodle flow? If the latter is the case, then simply removing the flow noodle accomplishes the same thing as disabling a node, doesn't it?

@{595459a74f08c21baf12e507|full_name}: It would work just like deleting the node, yes. The flow would stop, and the connected noodles would all be disabled and not functioning too. But importantly, these noodles are not disconnected. The point is to preserve node placement, and all of its connections while also being disabled. It's almost like you can "Think of it as a way of commenting out a node while leaving it in your code structure.."

> simply removing the flow noodle accomplishes the same thing as disabling a node, doesn't it?

"Simply" is an assumption. I think this sort of node disabling feature could be useful for situations where the connections are many, or messy, and you would rather comment (disable) that line or lines of code (node(s)) quick. - - (Not delete them and then have to keep in mind exactly all the things it was connected to and where they are in your un-zoomable graph.)

If you delete code and retype it while debugging, more power to you. I don't like to do that. I'd rather comment it out temporarily.

As I said in the OP (and just now added "optionally" to), a more complicated version of the "disable a node to 'comment' it out" would enable you to optionally allow flow, but other functions of the node would not execute or respond to noodles.

Comments in normal code don't necessarily halt code execution order the first time the compiler hits a comment. So this would optionally make it work like that, _flow wise_. But as I said above, I don't know if that is crazy. See: overly complicated.

For anyone still confused. This is requested ONLY for debugging purposes.

I used the term "commenting" because that is common terminology used for disabling code while not removing it in a program. Real Graph Comments are obviously different. They are not part of this.

title: Define own structures/classes (assembly only?)

comments.body: this would have to be done in a language that is compiled down to the assembly, classes and structs are mostly a language-based thing and aren't really supposed to be a feature in assembly, I'd say wait for a compiler for a language that has structs n classes

@{5b565300b13b3c741470153d|full_name}:  it can be done by language but performance and interoperability would take a great hit, with support from bytecode level (just how c#/java bytecode have it) you could later combine many scripts from different compilers and still be able to exchange objects between them. And performance of existing data structures in c# will be just much better than the one made in interpreted bytecode.

@{5b565300b13b3c741470153d|full_name}: I agree, RISC > CISC. What we really need are load and store operations for structure and array creation on the heap. https://feedback.vrchat.com/vrchat-udon-closed-alpha-feedback/p/load-and-store-operations

@{5cf63c84628159186a222bbe|full_name}: But this isn't raw assembly, we don't have access to memory or anything like that. to create structures you would need to generate shit tons of global variables, and is interpreted language so RISC is only hurting performance as less operations can be performed on native compiled side, and more must be interpreted.

Additionally in future it would be nice to be able to make calls cross-scripts, and with support for objects at language level we could exchange objects between scripts made with different compiler without worring about compatibility between them.

@{5a4aaf7f758fa46d131cd36b|full_name}: Excuse me, what? The whole point of having the UdonVM ops to handle this is so that they are optimized by the AOT compiler. That is incredibly easy for the compiler to do with all RISC ops by design of RISC architecture. The ability for deep optimizations is literally the primary motivation behind RISC (and one of many reasons it's often so power efficient in hardware). It is not, however, possible for good optimizations to occur with CISC ops as you are suggesting get added.

@{5cf63c84628159186a222bbe|full_name}: UdomVM is an interpreter, there are no further optimization done to udon bytecode. It's simple vm that iterate over opcodes on big switch with 10 possible bytecodes, including 2 noop bytecodes. And I don't ever expect to see any from vrchat team. So we will either get more opcodes, just like we have in other bytecode interpreted languages like java/c# (skipping the jit part that probably will never exit for udon) or we will have mess with shit tons of pre-declared global variables (and number of them is limited in VM to some constant) and no way to have common code that can be shared across different languages working on udonvm.

I don't know where you got the idea of AOT compilation for udon?

@{5a4aaf7f758fa46d131cd36b|full_name}: We are not talking about programs running in the UdonVM. I'm not sure where you got that idea. AOT is used to compile UdonVM and every op they add to it. Adding ops with inputs and outputs that are indeterminate at compile time (ie, what you're asking for with this feedback) will prevent AOT from performing many optimizations.

@{5a4aaf7f758fa46d131cd36b|full_name}: 
"RISC is only hurting performance as less operations can be performed on native compiled side, and more must be interpreted."
I don't think you quite understand what RISC even means. How could `ADD, output, arg1, arg2` that would run directly without needing function call through the interpreter be slower than 3 heap ops and a function call op `PUSH, arg1
 PUSH, arg2
 PUSH, output
 EXTERN, "SystemPrimitive.__op_Addition__SystemPrimitive_SystemPrimitive__SystemPrimitive`?

@{5cf63c84628159186a222bbe|full_name}: AOT already can't perform any advanced optimizations here, as it is used for dynamic scrips, so there isn't much to optimize. My proposed features don't need to be more "indeterminate" than existing opcodes, as could be implemented in similar/same way as current heap is implemented.

@{5cf63c84628159186a222bbe|full_name}: like with your exact example: udon does not have ADD operation, it can only execute externs, it does not have any instructions to operate on data. There is no "add" opcode. Everything is an extern. So yea, would also be nice to have more opcodes like ADD one too. Currently you can only load variables and execute externs.

@{5a4aaf7f758fa46d131cd36b|full_name}: That operation and other arithmetic, logic, and basic memory ops is what fundamental RISC is. I'm talking about optimizations within the UdonVM itself, not what the UdonVM runs. Any ops added to the vm should be highly optimizable, which is why I don't think any op should be handling structures that can't be determined when the UdonVM is compiled by the vrchat team.

@{5a4aaf7f758fa46d131cd36b|full_name}: Heap manipulation ops (load and store) would allow people creating compilers to choose how to create their own structures in memory and optimize based on the program being compiled. Removing the burden on the vrchat devs to create a complex assembler that attempts to handle the optimizations without knowledge of the program source being compiled.

@{5cf63c84628159186a222bbe|full_name}: just like heap content can't be determined when UdonVM is compiled, so in same way any current opcode, as all of them operate on this heap, it does not change anything here. So additional opcoded could be written in optimized form to perform some tasks, as AOT can't optimize our scripts more, but additional more specialized opcodes can.

Like in same way performance of string replace written on raw opcodes to iterate over chars of string on udonvm would be just horrible compared to single call to existing function in C# that was already optimized by AOT.

@{5cf63c84628159186a222bbe|full_name}: 
> creating compilers to choose how to create their own structures in memory
But we don't have access to memory, and each access is already costly due to additional scans and walls of ifs for each read and write. 
So when creating a compiler you can't really choose too much, as you are already limited by the VM. And lack of access to actual memory for sure will not change, so its better to get some more specialized operations.

@{5a4aaf7f758fa46d131cd36b|full_name}: Not quite. AOT cannot know the properties of that string and it is therefore not possible to optimize. However a compiler building directly for UdonVM and operating on a char array directly in udon heap would be able to determine what optimization if any to perform. The RISC ops such a compiler would use in the UdonVM would be so simple that AOT can actually optimize them very close to the hardware ops they represent.
@{5a4aaf7f758fa46d131cd36b|full_name}: A constant predetermined heap size would make performance a non-issue

@{5cf63c84628159186a222bbe|full_name}: 
> AOT cannot know the properties of that string and it is therefore not possible to optimize.

But it does not need to, c# string replace method will be already optimized by AOT, not for every possible string, but it will be simple machine code to perform an replace of string.

Where the version wrote on UdonVM using some compiler will still need to iterate on all opcodes, go thro a lot of branches on each heap read/write (and this will be performed for each char in  string). 

There is just no way for interpreted code to run here faster than native one, its a big and complex operation with a lot of reads and writes for udon. 

Expect for cases where compiler could just get rid of some replace function as result would be known at compile time, but thats an edge case that I would not expect to happen. As in most cases it will be dynamic string replaced by dynamic string, something that you can't optimize more than just replace logic itself.

details:
I'm trying to write a compiler for UdonVM, but the dynamic nature of EXTERN functions prevents us from writing a static analyzer (e.g. type checking).
We need at least:
- Names of EXTERNS
- API to get the following info per EXTERN:
    - expected types for each stack element in array
   - the usage per element, argument ("in" in C#) or overwritable argument ("ref" in C#) or return value ("out" in C#).
Documentation is not enough. We need a programmatical access for those information.
title: Request: Metadata of built-in EXTERNs for static analysis

comments.body: It seems like at least a portion of the types are taken from .NET and Unity libraries, so reflection will get you part of the way there.. Nodes in System seem to be in .NET's System namespace, and UnityEngine in Unity's UnityEngine namespace.

@{5b93e4741e75674a7ea03e2f|full_name}: Not quite, EXTERNs are provided via 

UdonExternDelegate IUdonWrapperModule.GetExternFunctionDelegate(string signature)

where UdonExternDelegate is (IUdonHeap heap, uint[] addresses) => void.

It's a function that takes the label and returns a corresponding delegate (if defined). Also, the format of label like "SystemConvert.__ToString__SystemInt32__SystemString" has nothing to do with the actual implementation of those wrappers.

It's also just a convention that the last address pushed to the stack is used to store a return value; wrappers can arbitrary read/write every address in the stack.

Summing up the discussion with Lyuma and JakEne on the Discord:

The label seems to follow the convention `<func-name>__<input-type1>_<input-type2>__<output-type>`, but we've found something weird. 

For example, `GameObject.Find (static method)` and `Transform.Find (instance method)` have the same-ish name `Find__SystemString__UnityEngineTransform` and `Find__SystemString__UnityEngineGameObject`.

JakEne says: "it does appear that all object methods have an implicit this (probably SystemObject type)".  This kind of inconsistency between static & instance method makes it hard to infer the actual type signature from the labels.

We, at least, need to create a strict and consistent convention for those EXTERN labels which is enough to extract the said informations, and make it documented, accessible via API (something like `string[] GetDefinedExternNames()`), and enforced.

My suggestion about the instance methods is to make it appear in the first argument of the signature so that everything looks like static methods.

For example, the signature corresponding to `Transform.Find (instance method)` would better be `Find__UnityEngineTransform_SystemString__UnityEngineTransform`.

Also, my proposed convention about EXTERNs which semantically have multiple outputs is to list all the `out` parameters at the end of the `__` separated list, so that `<func-name>__<input-type1>_<input-type2>__<output-type1>_<output-type2>`

For example, 
`SystemDateTime.__TryParse__SystemString_SystemIFormatProvider_SystemGlobalizationDateTimeStyles_SystemDateTimeRef__SystemBoolean`
should be instead named 
`SystemDateTime.__TryParse__SystemString_SystemIFormatProvider_SystemGlobalizationDateTimeStyles__SystemDateTime_SystemBoolean`.
since the 3rd and 4th address of the stack is used as output.

Sorry for another long post. From the documentation and actual extern labels, I guess the current convention is:

* For a static func from void to void, the label will be `__Foo__SystemVoid`. Let's call this *Type-S1*.
* For a static func from void to T, it will be `__Foo__T`. *Type-S2*.
* For a static func from T1,T2 to void, it will be `__Foo__T1_T2__SystemVoid`. *Type-S3*. 
* For a static func from T1,T2 to U, it will be `__Foo__T1_T2__U`. *Type-S4*.

Similarly, Type-I1 to Type-I4 is defined for instance functions.

Examples:
Type-S1: `SystemTimeZoneInfo.__ClearCachedData__SystemVoid`
Type-S2: `SystemBoolean.__get_TrueString__SystemString`
Type-S3: `UnityEngineAnimatorUtility.__OptimizeTransformHierarchy__UnityEngineGameObject_SystemStringArray__SystemVoid`
Type-S4: `SystemBoolean.__op_Equality__SystemBoolean_SystemBoolean__SystemBoolean`
Type-I1: `SystemTimeZoneInfoArray.__Initialize__SystemVoid`
Type=I2: `SystemBoolean.__ToString__SystemString`
Type-I3: `SystemBooleanArray.__Set__SystemInt32_SystemBoolean__SystemVoid`
Type-I4: `SystemBoolean.__Equals__SystemObject__SystemBoolean`

Also, for label `L`, `GetExternFunctionParameterCount(L)` returns the number of stacks the extern func is expecting.
Let's call it an *arity* of `L`.

Type-S1 funcs have arity 0. S2 have 1. S3 have n where n is the number of arguments. S4 have n+1.

On the other hand, instance funcs have an implicit argument corresponding to the instance. So I1 have 1, I2 have 2, I3 have n+1, and I4 have n+2.
It follows that we can distinguish between Type-Sk and Type-Ik funcs by looking at their arity.

**There are 1069 (out of 21390) externs which contradict to the convention.**

For example, `UnityEngineAnimationsAimConstraint.__GetComponent__T` should have an arity 1 (if static) or 2 (if instance), but it has 3.

Another example is `VRCSDKBaseInputManager.__get__IsUsingHandController__SystemFuncSystemBoolean`.
This has an arity 1. I suspect that the `__` between `get` and `IsUsing..` is a duplicate, and it should just be `_` so that it now becomes Type-S2.

---

The list of inconsistent functions is available here: https://gist.github.com/cannorin/0233147a6a5c3855c727ef9934f1108e

Also, here is the list of every function and its type (warning: it's very large): https://gist.github.com/cannorin/031aec897dd739791a115d18c82b1d90

Supporting Shader would allow us people who write shaders access to use global variables in shaders such as SetGlobalColor and SetGlobalFloat. This would allow for more creativity and flexibility in creating more intricate shaders for the community.
In fact, in some instances it is impossible to write a shader without access to these methods. For example, some shaders use an addpass and basemap shader, however due to Unity's implementation, the shader's properties in the inspector cannot reach past the initial main shader, and the additional 2 shaders have no access to the properties, thus limiting the ability to customize the shaders. This could easily be taken care of if global variables were supported.
The only current solution to this problem is to create a script added to the object, which allows to set the value, and hard codes (writes the value) into the actual file when it's changed. Quite ugly and clunky workaround.
We could seriously use this, please hear us VRChat team
https://docs.unity3d.com/ScriptReference/Shader.html

As of build 1258, we're now able to globally declare variables, so long as the variable names have the prefix "_Udon". However, that leaves the second half of this canny unattended to, that being the global keywords.
It's still not possible to declare global keywords. Which means we've either got to use dynamic branching or manual variants for cases where it's not possible to assign keywords directly, e.g. replacement shaders. And for the cases where we can set keywords on materials, we'd still have to loop over every material in order to enable/disable it for all of them.
The main concern with global keywords is probably the global keyword limit though, so maybe that'll have to wait until VRChat migrates to Unity 2021.2 or greater.

When using a subgraph multiple times within the same for loop, the Udon VM exits with error code 1 at the end of the first loop. A sample of the graph and subgraph can be seen in the images below. 
Calling the subgraph in sequence without a for loop runs as expected. Having only one subgraph call per loop works as expected.
Upon closer inspection of the Udon Assembly code, the JUMP address at the end of the for loop 0x000053 does not correspond to the start of the for loop that increments the index, but another code segment. 
After modifying the bytecode in the .asset file to correspond to the correct JUMP address of 0x00002F, the code runs as expected.

details:
This is a data handling paradigm which may help to simplify logic; I have used it quite successfully in my own language projects.  The concept is simple:  Every data value (noodle) could potentially have a value of "null".  This includes nominal value types like int, float, etc.  Every node which takes input(s) checks to see if any of those inputs are null, and acts appropriately.  Most of this time, "acts appropriately" means outputting null for their outputs, but not necessarily.
There are several advantages to this approach:
Being a mostly non-interactive medium (in the sense that there's no terminal to readily display errors on), having a node output nulls is a way of signalling that an error has occurred, without disrupting the execution of the program, particularly in cases where the error is nonfatal. It allows for the easy communication of errors.  Operations which would operate normally without errors, can be bypassed when errors are present, and those errors are propagated on until they are handled.
For example, if you have an array index node, inputs being an array and an index in that array, output being the item at that index, then the output would be null if the input array is null, or the input index is null, or the index is invalid.
The program can then handle this case by checking to see if the output is null; if it is null, it knows that something has gone wrong and can act accordingly.  It generally doesn't care *why* it went wrong, only that it did.
Implementing this also covers several suggestions in this board:

https://feedback.vrchat.com/vrchat-udon-closed-alpha-feedback/p/a-is-valid-branch-node (Null Convention essentially implements this)
https://feedback.vrchat.com/vrchat-udon-closed-alpha-feedback/p/add-an-optional-parameter-to-custom-event (Null Convention for cases where there isn't a parameter)
https://feedback.vrchat.com/vrchat-udon-closed-alpha-feedback/p/request-add-list-type-handling (Null Convention deals with cases where one attempts to read a list at an invalid index)

Handling these errors takes the form of nodes which do not automatically output nulls when they receive one.  The most basic of these would be the Coalesce operation; the Coalesce operation takes two or more inputs, and returns the first input which is not null.  
Another is a basic IsNull, which returns true if the input is null, or false if it is anything other than null.
title: Null Convention

details:
Posting this here as Ron suggested it: "If you feel strongly about an aspect of UDON or concerned about security or moderation aspect write it up in feedback."
With the power that Udon wields, we must all understand that some community members will exploit it. Udon won't always be used for good. This is why effective community moderation (and thusly effective moderators when ranked users report issues) is extremely important. I think those in staff that aren't working on the dev side of things really need to prioritize conceptualizing intelligent enforcement of 'bad eggs' so when devs are available, they are ready to act on tooling enforcement.
They don't need to do this alone. The community needs to be able to find/identify these bad eggs and moderators with the help of development staff need to create effective, understandable rules and tools to carry out enforcement. These tools need to be dynamic, prioritized for enforcement based on weights of the accused and the accuser[s] at the very least.
The "Trusted" rank is not a good tool to define who is actually trusted and not a good starting point for weights. It may be a meme at this point but "Trusted users are more cancerous than new users in VRChat in 2019. Trusted is a synonym for untrustworthy."
I believe that Community Labs was a good example of poor enforcement practices at VRChat. The moderators probably are doing their best, I can't see within the veil, but I don't believe they have the tools to properly carry out enforcement. 'Bad eggs' continue to post rule-breaking worlds, they are reported, they may be disciplined, who knows, but they come back later to continue with earnest.
Udon has power to influence the VRChat experience moreso than anything VRChat has ever done, ever. Will it come in as a semi-rogue but extremely positive experience, or will it be something that cripples the communities trust of VRChat for a very long time? I would block a full-blown release until you have the tools to make sure this doesn't happen.
title: [META] How Udon Will Be Moderated Should Be a Release Blocker.

comments.body:
-Make reports system actually work instead of ignoring reported worlds with 10-20+ reports for crashers and malicious content
-Hire more moderators and pick trustworthy community moderators, and give them the ability to remove bad/malicious worlds and avatars
-Rework trust system, currently trusted users are more likely to be malicious than new users, add much more "space" between the ranks to reduce amount of trusted users (should take 1-2 years for trusted) and increase amount of new user/user/known users. Trusted should be very old accounts/players
-Make automatic world approval from labs -> public, be more strict instead of letting the system publicize worlds while ignoring multiple reports on the worlds
-Less temporary bans for crashers and malicious content, more permanent bans

While I agree that world moderation needs to be better, reporting a world for it being malicious, then seeing it public 10 minutes later, really feels pretty bad, I don't think this has anything to do with Udon at all. If you want to make a 0.1MB world that will instantly crash someone, you can do that now. Udon seems really irrelevant to this discussion

I do think that reporting worlds needs to be more heavily weighted when the automatic system decides if a world leaves labs to public
VRChat has a deeply rooted moderation problem that staff tries to treat as a content problem.  Udon and what bad things will be done with it is only a small part of a larger problem.

title: Load and Store operations

details:
Currently all variables need to be defined at the beginning of assembly, this creates many issues and mess when trying to implement normal support for methods, especially when trying to add recursion in some sane way, as simulating stack on this heap is pretty nasty.
So would be great to get support for stack memory with bytecodes to load/store variable probably with some way to define size of stack for event/method.
Like this: 
```
.code_start
    
// simillar to externs, _<name>__<arguments>__<returnType>
_addInts__SystemInt_SystemInt__SystemInt:
    .stackSize 3
    loadInt 0 // first argument 
    loadInt 1 // second argument 
    extern natveAdd
    returnInt
// and calling them
_update:
    .stackSize 2
    storeInt 0 3 // store 3 at index 0
    storeInt 1 6
    call _addInts__SystemInt_SystemInt__SystemInt
    // now there is 9 at index 0
```
gist: https://gist.github.com/1504602ba979c8fd02749ed8c1f81f80
And this would be even better with support for custom structures (that can be implemented just as some custom object that stores type name and map of parameters)

This would help a lot with creation of custom compilers and making the resulting code being fast.  Currently we are really limited to create anything that would allow to create more complex scripts.

details:
I understand this is a pretty loud headline, but these are the thoughts that came into my head after meeting Udon.
I will try to explain what makes Udon bad both in pov of the general concept and in pov of implementation. I think it is important to say this right now, becuause Udon is not yet complete and in active development, I hope to influence the way it develops.
Also I am sorry for my English, as I am not English-speeking and I did not happen to learn English thoroughly.
~ ~ ~
First, why flow/node-based programming at all? It seems, the main goal of developers is to make a simple mechanism for creating game logic that will allow a wide range of creators to quickly and without special knowledge to implement their ideas.
In practice, it turns out that you still need to know the basics of C# and programming in general. It's not that you need to know the Unity Scripting API, of course, for Unity you need to know this. The point is that Udon stands on C#/Mono, and this is clearly visible in Udon programs. Now Udon looks like an alternative and not complete syntax for C#/CIL, it does not give the opportunity to abstract from C# internals and standards. It does not gives you simple types such as simple integer and floating numbers, strings, lists and tables as it in popular scripting languages such as python/lua/js/..., instead of it gives you full-range of internal types with own low-level specifics (and actually not all of it acessible right now), It does not gives you simple ways to play with collections and opertaions, such as foreach/where/select...  (and actually no collections at all right now), It does not gives you abstract simple and helpful functions/methods (for now). It is literraly asks you to call each (internal) operation manually and you need to know how to do that. It's like you re-writing CIL bytecode visually.
So, what we got? For newbies Udon is too complex. I heared from a lot of friends both who does not have real programming experience, and who have some lua/js/python experience, that Udon is too complex and hard to understand. On the other hand, I see there is a lot of skilled people in community who mostly understands Udon, but they complain about visual programming. For them it's much easier to write text. We already see how ppl trying to make own ways to generate Udon asm to avoid visual scripting at all. (Thank you guys, my respects for your work) It really harder to make some complex logics visually, than by writing text.

~ ~ ~

Second, let's compare node/visual with same for shaders. I often hear Udon comparisons with things as Shader Graph (in future Unities), Amplify Sheder Editor, Shader Forge, Unreal Engine shader editor and similar. Well... Shaders (common) does not have global state while executing, it's is more like microchip code that have entire enironment to play with. So, for example, If I use any fuction such as UnityObjectToClipPos multiple times on same data, HLSL compiller can optimize it into single call, because these function calls doesn't change anything globally. More of that, even if it changes something, compiller can deal with it as all function inlined (in basic shaders w/o new modern fancy features). That's not because HLSL cmpillers super smart or somethig, that's because shading languages have simple design. In Udon/C# stands on Mono, each call is unitary, can change anything globally and compiller can not deal with it and suggest optimizations. Why I pointing this out? For example not so long ago, Error.mdl tried to make one thing that involves file reading ( https://ptb.discordapp.com/channels/189511567539306508/657394924433571870/657813419050795018 , https://cdn.discordapp.com/attachments/657394924433571870/657813411631071242/spagettiknots.jpg ) and noticed it works very slow. If you see carefully, you may notice: there is not obious when "Text Asset Read Bytes" and "Byte[] Get" evaluated, thats problem here (I believe, but sure, as I didn't tested this, lul). But same thing with sahders should works very well. Issue here not with Udon compiller - same can be happen with any other compiller. It's not possible to auto-optimize here, as underlying sofware does not know how these actions affect app environment gloablly. This is a job for programmer. When we writing C# we probably will do something like: byte[] data_that_i_need = my_text_asset_variable.get_bytes(); (Actually just my_text_asset_variable.bytes, as it is property, which is also not obivous, so it is a bad example, but this is another story, I hope u got the point) and then using this data_that_i_need in futher code. In Flow/nodes scripting you have feeling that you can just connect these nodes and that's all, but this is not. You just shoot you leg and didn't noticed how! I want to point out here, that there is actually two kind of flows: data flow and and execution flow, which often non-linear!. Shader basically math-based, developer tells how one color/position vectors should be transformed into other vectors and executing order and path does not (always) matter, and no need to think about global states (as I pointed before), also branhing in shaders very rare. So yea, I want to tell that flow/node based is bad choice for logical programming over global game state. 

You may think: Are you againtst visual programming? Want to force everyone to write text? No. Actually, there is a lot of forms for visual coding. My favorite one design is puzzle-like block nodes, which is popular to teach children the basics of programming. Just google "visual programming", there is a lot of various products!

~ ~ ~

Third, lets talk a bit about Udon ASM and Udon VM. These things. I do not understand why it exist. I have an assumption that devs wanted to create something like a sandbox/security-filter, but instead created monster. I believe this unnecesary layers that create large overhead and way to make 1000 and 1 more hard-to-cathch annoyng bugs in future. More complex something, easier to make misatake, easier to break. For now I don't see what Udon VM can do that is not possible with usual C#/Mono assemblies. You may think? What is another way? You want to allow everyone write whatever they want and execute on other's computers dircetly without any control? Yes and No. You may think it's hard to validate DLLs for various malicious things that creator might make. I want to tell you why it's actually easier than by doing own assembly/compilation/vm system.

Mono assembly is not like common PE assemply. Mono assembly, to put it simple, more like encoded into interpreter-readable usual text-code you writen. It is very high-level abstarction. It does not describes operations on "pure memory" and "pure processor instructions sequence". It is not C/C++, Mono assembly holds a lot of data! It holds everything: types, methods, fields, references to types, references to methods, references to fields, generics, boxing/unboxing and so on, almost no raw data. More of that, there is explicit and strict border between managed and unmanaged, safe and unsafe things. Take a look at any random program writen in C# for Unity (Mono) and take a look at this reference https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_CIL_instructions . Let's ignore basic branch/math/conversion ops, and take a look how program intercats with globals using object-instructions.
Method call? It's call/callvirt, operand type - <method> which is token, which is described in meta of assemly where all references stored. We looking at method this uder this toking and see, for example, creator calling forbidden method. No need to deal with any kind of adresses to strange raw virtual method tables or something. Field access? Same: ldsfld/ldsflda/stfld/stsfld, same: we can see what this token for and check permissions. We see creator using unsafe operaions? Pointers? Allocations? StructLayout? Ban. Easy.
You might think: Isnt its hard to parse assemblies? No. I had experience with Mono.Cecil ( https://www.mono-project.com/docs/tools+libraries/libraries/Mono.Cecil/ ) - it can parse relativly large DLLs into object model for edits or checks in a couple of seconds, even on my weak laptop, basic scripts for worlds should work in fractions of a second, so validation might be both on a server and on a client at world-loading.
I believe, it's much easier to allow scripting for comunity and make CIL opcodes filter, to ban everything complex and perform whitelisting. It's much easier to maintain this, than that large Udon ASM/compiller/VM elephant, and no any extra overhead at runtime! Am I wrong? I suggest to try to write something malicious in comments using only common instructions. For now I know only ways is to make too large arrays and collections, but, I believe same works in Udon (need extra tests).

More of thiat, I know C#/.NET standard provides security control that also covers CIL/MSIL code, which is also supported in Mono. I have no experience with this, so I do not make statements about this. But I know for sure, it's possible to define various security/trust levels and evaluate code with different permissions, to achive somethig like sandboxed envioronment. I going to google more about that so may be I alter this thought.

It hurts me the most that fact community wants to just write C# code, but insted of just build mono assemblies we going to invent own bicycles to generate Udon ASM without any guarantees and support and with risk (as it's unofficial tools), without any way to debug, with higer possiblities of bugs because of complexity, with overhead that will reduce performance, without any cool unique things from UdonVM. It is cool devs allows to make custom asm compillers, but it looks more like: "If u dont like to connect blocks using lines, then here get our instructions set, do what ever you want with these, invent own bicycles, we dont care. And yea we going to change this, so things will randomly got broken in future." I am rly sad and dissapointed about this. 

~ ~ ~

Fourth, I not sure how to explain that, Udon not so powerful in building large structures, it does not gives you feeling of real development environment. It feels morle like writing Windows commandline shell scripts, but visually. We working with concepts of "Objects", but we dont have fundamental concepts of object-oriented programming: encapsulation, inheritance and polymorphism. You can not define own types, and even if it will be possible in future, it does not feels like it will be possible to extend types, use all power of polymorphism, which can be important for implementing complex game logics and mechanics. We can not even call Udon functional as it does not have "pure" functions! Yea, we have SubGraphs but we dont have contextual I/O for that. We need to set global instance variables and "call" subgraph using events (messages) which is really cringy. Can we get at least ok-implemented functions?

~ ~ ~

So my suggestions to improve:
- In Node Graphs: Make a lot of abstarctions and helper operations to make things actually simplier for newbies. May be "Udon commons library" or something.
- In Node Graphs: Make execution path for absolutely every node, so it's execution time and order will be explicit and obvious, even with even if you have to sacrifice convenience of "free nodes".
- In Node Graphs: Make easier read/write to local variables, for caching data in data flow to avoid unnecesary geters calls, also here:
- - Make nodes inputs/outputs not only flow lines and user-given statics, but also with inplace variable selector, so creators can read/write variables directly in node without creating tons of extra get/set nodes.
- In Node Graphs: Probably make nodes puzzle-like for execution path, so it's easier to control flow order. Or do something with flow control, to make it in way that gives less possibilities to do something wrong.
- If it's possible throw away ASM/VM and compile Udon nodes directly into CIL. Allow custom user-provided CIL asms. Validate CIL on both server and client for blacklisted/malicious operations using analysis tools. Setup kind of sandboxed environment using security API for creators scripts execution.
- If not, then make official and maintained way for compiling C#/CIL into Udon ASM, so community can write C# scripts without depending on 3rd tools. Improve Udon to be more close to CIL, with custom functions and types, with power of OOP concepts.

comments.body: The text is longer and more messy than I expected. Therefore, later, I will probably make some changes and comments.

While I do agree with you on points one and two, I have to disagree on point three, and point four kinda falls away with my stance on point three.

When I first heard about Udon, I was very sceptical.  But once I saw the existance of Udon Assembly (which I'll refer to as Udon Intermediate Language, or UIL, because that's closer to what it actually is) that they seem to be open in terms of architecture, including outright ecouraging external compilers, I did see a spark of hope.  It leads me to think that, perhaps, someone on the team had actually taken a compiler course, and there was hope for them yet.

There are many posts talking about defining structures, or adding opcodes for arithemetic operations, etc.  They are all missing the point.  Those are all abstractions.  It doesn't matter if you have one structured variable, or a dozen non-structured ones. It doesn't matter if you have 100 opcodes all doing different things, or ten opcodes and all of the interesting things are what amount to function calls.  Any decent compiler can optimize for all of that.  Do you think that the C executable running knows or cares whether the int it's doing calculations on is in a structure? No. It just knows "add the value in this register to that register and put it in this other register" or "get this value from this spot in memory and put it here".  It doesn't care if the code it's executing exists in a subroutine, or a method, or a lambda, or a closure, or any of the dozens of things that all basically mean the same thing in practice.

It doesn't matter (for the most part) if the IL uses three opcodes to add two numbers, or thirty.  The only place where that matters is in the compiler.  If the compiler is good, it'll get rid of all of the extra and boil it down to the exact bytecodes that need to be sent to the processor to accompish the task at hand.

We should also bear in mind that speed is not the only design concern here.  Safety is another important design concern.  If these programs are transmitted in IL, and compiled in place on the client side, ensures that the barrier toward getting malicious executable code running in the process space is much higher.  All of this talk about "just allow C# scripts" seems to miss this point.  Yes, it's certainly possible to scan C# source, or compiled CIL, to see if anything looks suspcious, but it is not an easy task.  The only options down that road are either to A) allow for the possibility of malicious code, which is completely unacceptable; B) require C# scripts be so simple that they might as well be this node-based language we're already complaining about; or C) spend significant amounts of time and resources writing an execution analysis engine that might not even be possible (see also, the Halting Problem).  That's not even getting into the problems associated with trying to write code for execution on multiple platforms (in this case, .NET and Android).

Or, you design your own IL.  You can design that IL to preclude most of the actively harmful things that a malicious party could do.  And then when you compile that IL into executable code it's quite easy to insert your own code to guard against those situations which are harder to detect with code analysis.  And then you can compile it at runtime to the appropriate platform.

For an example of that, look at infinite loops. Having loops available in the language is very useful, but having infinite loops is difficult.  Now, if the language is interpreted, then infinite loops are easily delt with; the interpreter simply stops after a period of time.  But of course, interpretation is not desirable from a speed perspective.  When the language is compiled directly, it's much more difficult to see if a loop is infinite. I'm not saying that can't be managed, but it's a lot more difficult.  With a custom compiled IL (especially one as basic as UIL), the compiler can insert code before every JUMP instruction that moves backwards in the file.  Then, if this code is executed too many times, it can be interuppted by the runtime, just as in the interpreted case, but without the added overhead.

Of course, all of this assumes that UIL will be compiled at some point.  While I know from my own experience that this is entirly possible (the ERP [Enterprise Resource Planning] software I wrote and have actively maintained for the last ten years uses the same techniques that could be used in this situation), I do assume that the devs will be using these techniques.  I understand that this is not a safe assumption.  I saw a glimmer of hope; I've not yet seen proof of hope.

I recommend to anyone who's interested in compiler design, "Compilers: Principles, Techniques, and Tools" by Aho, Sethi, and Ullman (And Lam) (1st ed: 9780201100884, 2nd ed: 9780321486813), which I've found to be an invaluable resource over the years.  While the second edition might be newer, I've gotten quite a lot of use out of the first edition, which can be had on Amazon for as little as $4.


As for your list of suggestions (in order):

- Many of these abstractions can (and I'm confidant, will) be provided by compiler writers.

- Execution path should only be for nodes that have non-deterministic or time-relevant side-effects.  If anything, this means that fewer nodes should have execution path arrows.  This current node language has a fair bit of functional aspect to it.

- Again, this will be delt with by compilers.

- Syntactic sugar, but still a good suggestion.

- Not sure what this one means.

- Absolutely not, for the reasons explained above.

- See above.
